name: Jury Selection and Public Data
title: Jury Selection and Public Data
answer: Jury selection and public data covers the use of publicly available records to inform decisions about which potential jurors to strike, keep, or question further. This includes voter registration files, property records, campaign contributions, social media posts, court records, and news coverage. The work sits within litigation prediction and judicial analytics because it tries to estimate how a juror may lean based on observable public signals. It does not replace voir dire, but it gives trial teams a structured view of the pool before questioning begins.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Jury selection and public data covers the use of publicly available records to inform decisions about which potential jurors to strike, keep, or question further. This includes voter registration files, property records, campaign contributions, social media posts, court records, and news coverage. The work sits within litigation prediction and judicial analytics because it tries to estimate how a juror may lean based on observable public signals. It does not replace voir dire, but it gives trial teams a structured view of the pool before questioning begins.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on standard cloud infrastructure with databases that store and index large collections of public records. Data pipelines pull from government portals, commercial aggregators, and social media APIs where terms of service allow. Entity resolution systems match names, addresses, and other identifiers to link records to specific individuals in the jury pool. Access is usually restricted to the legal team, with logging and encryption to protect case strategy and personal data.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Analysts first collect public data for each person on the jury list, then clean and normalize it into a single profile. Natural language processing extracts topics, sentiment, and affiliations from posts, comments, and public statements. Statistical models compare these profiles to outcomes in similar past cases or to known attitudinal markers, producing a risk or affinity score for each juror. The scores are used to prioritize follow up questions during voir dire, not to make automatic strikes.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are privacy, accuracy, and fairness. Public records can be outdated, mismatched, or taken out of context, and social media posts may not reflect a person's actual views. Many jurisdictions restrict how lawyers may investigate jurors or what data they may use, and some bar contact with jurors or their networks. Provenance matters because a model's output is only as good as the source data, and hidden bias in that data can lead to discriminatory strikes. Teams typically document where each data point came from and how it was used, and courts may ask for that record.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Public data will keep growing, and models will get better at linking records across sources and detecting stale or false information. Courts and legislatures are likely to add rules about what public data can be used in jury selection and how it must be disclosed. The field may move toward real time monitoring of public posts during trial, though that raises new ethical questions. Human review will remain central because jury decisions are too high stakes to leave to an automated score alone.
